title: Fractions: Multiply & Divide
subtitle: Multiplying is easier than adding. Dividing is a flip away.
objectives: Multiply a fraction by a whole number or mixed number
Explain why multiplying by a fraction makes a number smaller
Divide by a fraction using the reciprocal
Explain why dividing by a fraction makes a number bigger
Cancel before multiplying to keep numbers small

cards.title: This one is easier than last week
cards.text: No common denominator. No re-cutting. Multiply the tops, multiply the bottoms, and you are done.

cards.title: Straight across
cards.text: There is no trick and no special case. It works for every pair of fractions.

cards.title: Why straight across is correct
cards.text: Tap through all four. The last one is dividing, and it is the surprising one.

cards.title: A whole number is a fraction with 1 underneath
cards.text: That one move turns every mixed problem into the straightforward case.
points: **Never multiply the wholes separately.** That fails.

cards.title: Gear ratios multiply, one after another
cards.text: The gearbox ratio and the final drive ratio multiply together to give what actually reaches the wheels.
points: **Change either one** and the result changes.
**Tuning screens do this arithmetic** every time.
**Fractions are ratios**, which is why it is the same sum.

cards.title: Multiplying by less than one makes it smaller
cards.text: You met this with decimals in Week 5. It is exactly the same fact, wearing fractions.
points: **"Of" means multiply.** Half of eight is four.
**An improper fraction** grows it, as usual.

cards.title: Good spot to pause
cards.text: Multiplying done. Part 2 is dividing, which is one flip away from what you just learned. Your place is saved.

cards.title: Nobody divides by a fraction. They flip it and multiply
cards.text: That sounds like a shortcut that shouldn't work. It works, and the picture in the figure shows why.

cards.title: Flip the second one, then multiply
cards.text: The reciprocal of a fraction is that fraction upside down. Dividing by a number is the same as multiplying by its reciprocal.
points: **Only the second fraction flips.** Never the first.

question.explain: Turn it upside down. The reciprocal of 3/4 is 4/3.

cards.title: Dividing asks how many fit inside
cards.text: 3 ÷ 1/2 is asking how many halves fit into three. Six do, so the answer is bigger than what you started with.
points: **Say the question out loud.** It stops being strange.
**Dividing by something small** gives a lot of them.
**Dividing by less than 1 always grows the number.**

cards.title: How many stacks is that?
cards.text: You have 3 stacks and you want to split them into quarter-stacks. Dividing by a quarter tells you how many you get.
points: **Nothing was created.** It was just recounted.
**That is all dividing by a fraction is.**

question.explain: Flip the second: 2/3 × 6/1 = 12/3 = 4. Four sixths fit into two thirds.

cards.title: Cancel before you multiply
cards.text: If a top and a bottom share a factor, divide both by it first. The numbers stay small and the answer arrives simplified.

cards.title: Splitting a round into working intervals
cards.text: A three-minute round divided into thirty-second bursts. That is a division by a fraction of a minute, and coaches do it constantly.
points: **The answer got bigger** and nothing was added.
**You have counted this** without calling it division.

question.text: Dividing a number by 1/4 makes it four times bigger.
question.explain: True. You are counting how many quarters fit inside, and four fit into each whole.

terms.def: A fraction turned upside down. The reciprocal of 2/3 is 3/2.
Dividing a top and a bottom by a shared factor before multiplying.
In fraction problems, 'of' means multiply. Half of eight is 1/2 × 8.
Top bigger than bottom. Convert mixed numbers to these before multiplying.

cards.title: The four that matter
points: **A whole number is that number over 1.**
**Divide: flip the second one, then multiply.**
**Below 1 shrinks when you multiply, grows when you divide.**

quiz.explain: 3/15 straight across, which simplifies to 1/5. Cancelling the 3s first is quicker.
4 is 4/1, so 12/8, which simplifies to 3/2 or 1½.

quiz.text: Multiplying a number by 2/3 makes it smaller.
quiz.explain: True. 2/3 is less than one, so the answer is smaller than what you started with.

quiz.explain: Turn it upside down. Dividing by 5/8 is the same as multiplying by 8/5.

quiz.text: Dividing by a fraction smaller than 1 gives a bigger answer.
quiz.explain: True. You are counting how many small pieces fit inside, so there are a lot of them.

quiz.text: In 5/6 × 3/10, which pair can you cancel first?
options: The 3 and the 6, and the 5 and the 10
quiz.explain: 3 and 6 share 3; 5 and 10 share 5. That leaves 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4.
quiz.objective: Cancel before multiplying to keep numbers small

quiz.explain: 15/60 simplifies to 1/4. Cancelling first gets you there without the big numbers.

teacher.summary: Week 8 Math covers multiplying and dividing fractions, completing the four operations. It opens by pointing out that this week is easier than last week, which is true and worth saying: multiplication needs no common denominator at all. The fractionOps figure builds the area model in three taps so that 'multiply straight across' is demonstrated rather than asserted, and its fourth state answers the harder question of why dividing by a fraction makes a number bigger. Both traps from the decimals work in Week 5 return here in fraction form and are named as the same fact, so the two topics reinforce rather than compete. Cancelling before multiplying is included because it is the difference between an answer and an arithmetic mess.
discussion: Ask him why multiplying fractions needs no common denominator when adding does. The area model answers it.
Ask him to say '3 divided by a half' out loud as a question. How many halves fit into three is the whole idea.
Ask what 'of' means in a maths question. Half of eight is a multiplication, and naming that saves marks.
Ask him to do 5/6 × 3/10 twice, once with cancelling and once without. The second way is instructive.
teacher.extension: Have him scale a recipe by 2/3 and then by 3/2 and check he gets back to the original. Reciprocals become obvious when they undo each other.
misconceptions: 'You need a common denominator to multiply.' You do not. That is only for adding and subtracting.
'Multiplying always makes numbers bigger.' Multiplying by a fraction under 1 makes them smaller.
'Flip both fractions when dividing.' Only the second one. The first stays as it is.
'Cancelling changes the answer.' It is simplifying early. The answer is identical, and the numbers stay manageable.
